catalog_quote: All words in Slovene that are not clitics have at least one prominent syllable. Prominence is lexically determined, i.e., it is not predictable, so it is a feature of the word which must be learned along with the segmental sequence and the meaning. Prominence is marked in at least two broadly different ways depending on which dialect area a Slovene speaker comes from. Speakers from Ljubljana, the Upper and Lower Carniolan dialects, or the Carinthian dialect may have a pitch-accent (“tonemic”) system. Speakers from other areas generally have a dynamic stress (“stress”) system. In both the tonemic and stress systems, vestiges of a quantity opposition in stressed syllables may still be realized in many speakers’ systems. With the exception of some peripheral dialects, distinctions between long and short stressed syllables occur in the final or only syllable. ... Stress placement, vowel qua…
sweep_summary: Three title-hits for Slovenian. (1) Greenberg 2003 (STUF) — obtained (KU ScholarWorks copy via the Internet Archive; KU blocks our network) and read: word stress is assigned by a morpheme-level lexical accent algorithm (stress on the first rising-accented morpheme, falling accent shifts right, short final stress retracts), stress is not fixed to any position, and stress placement is the primary word-prosodic contrast in every Slovene system — CONFIRMS the catalog's 'lexical' coding (same author as the deciding Greenberg 2006 grammar; peer-reviewed corroboration, does not supersede the grammar's plainer statement). (2) Šekli 2010 (SSJLK 46, open PDF from centerslo.si; Šekli sole author, Smole is the compilers) — read: Standard Slovene verb stress is organized into lexical accent paradigms with root vs. infinitive/present-suffix stress and infinitive/present alternations (mériti mérim, nosíti nósim, moríti morím); REFINES the catalog's classification with the morphological structure of verb stress. (3) Vermeer 1986 (De Gruyter sandhi volume) — paywalled (30 EUR, no repository copy, no abstract); comparative prosodic-sandhi accentology, unlikely to be the best stress statement; priority low. discovery used Unpaywall/OpenAlex/OpenAIRE/Semantic Scholar APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: The surface accentual properties of words can be determined by an algorithm applied in the concatenation of individual morphemes, each of which is marked or unmarked for an underlying prosodic feature. [...] (1) Place of stress is assigned to the first rising-pitch morpheme, pitch in the remaining morphemes of these word-forms is ignored; (2) Any remaining falling pitch is shifted one syllable to the right [...]; (4) Short final stress is retracted one syllable, yielding rising pitch on that syllable. [...] In each type, stress placement is ranked above pitch and vowel quantity, which depend on the place of stress.
new_statements.citation: Greenberg, Marc L. 2003. Word prosody in Slovene from a typological perspective. STUF – Sprachtypologie und Universalienforschung 56(3): 234–251. doi:10.1524/stuf.2003.56.3.234 (author copy KU ScholarWorks hdl:1808/5245, archived copy (Internet Archive, 21 Apr 2024))
new_statements.locator: §3 'Lexical assignment of accent', p. 238; §10 Conclusion, p. 247
new_statements.reading: Peer-reviewed, first-hand statement by the same author as the catalog's deciding source: Slovene stress placement is determined by underlying lexical accent marks on morphemes (first rising-accented morpheme gets the stress, with rightward shift of falling accent and retraction of short final stress), not by a phonological edge rule; pitch and quantity are subordinate to the place of stress in every Slovene system (standard and dialects). This is a lexical/morphological accent system = catalog classification lexical. Šekli 2010 (pp. 141–142) independently shows the same for verbs: stress types with root vs. suffix stress and infinitive/present alternations (nosíti ~ nósim).

new_statements.quote: In the illustrative wordlists and the transcribed passage below certain syllables have been marked as stressed. These stressed syllables are characterized by greater duration as well as by amplitude and pitch prominence. Non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable. Stress placement is not predictable but is also rarely distinctive in Slovene, although in a few instances different forms of the same noun or verb differ only in stress placement, e.g.: ['stua:ri], [stua'ri:], stvari ('things', dual vs plural), ['no:simo], [no'si:mo], nosimo ('carry' 1st p. pl. indicative and imperative). [p. 88] Standard Slovene distinguishes two pitch accents, traditionally referred to as the 'acute' and the 'circumflex' accents, and these accents are tied to the location of stress. [p. 89]
new_statements.citation: Šuštaršič, Rastislav, Smiljana Komar & Bojan Petek. 1995. Slovene (Illustrations of the IPA). JIPA 25(2): 86-90. doi:10.1017/S0025100300005211

Only differences are scanned artefacts ([cno:simo] for ['no:simo]) which the compiler silently normalised. Section read in full: stressed = long…
new_statements.relation_note: Independent phoneticians' statement 'Stress placement is not predictable' matches the catalog's lexical coding (Greenberg 2006 'Prominence is lexically determined, i.e., it is not predictable') and the Greenberg 2003 lexical-accent statement; adds the pitch accent (acute/circumflex) detail and the note that stress is rarely distinctive. Suitable as a second citation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard Slovene (Ljubljana speakers) has one stressed syllable per non-compound word; its position is not predictable from phonological form (so it must be learned lexically) and is only rarely contrastive, though minimal pairs exist (stvari dual vs plural, nosimo indicative vs imperative). Stressed vowels are long, unstressed short (length no longer distinctive for most speakers). On the stressed syllable two pitch accents (acute = rising/low, circumflex = falling/high) are distinguished, tied to the stress location, seldom lexically distinctive, and some standard speakers lack the distinction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the authors state only that non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable (compounds implicitly may have more).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-only minimal pairs: stvari ['stua:ri] dual vs [stua'ri:] plural; nosimo ['no:simo] indicative vs [no'si:mo] imperative. pitch accent minimal pair kila 'hernia' (acute) vs kila 'kilo' (circumflex); many words vary in accent and some speakers make no accent distinction.
new_statements.identity_note: Šuštaršič, Komar & Petek 1995 describe Standard Slovene as spoken by educated speakers, recorded from two Ljubljana speakers. Božič 2015 describes Novo mesto Slovenian, the Dolenjska (Lower Carniolan) dialect of the south-east, from the author's own native judgements checked with two or three other speakers; he explicitly compares it with Standard Slovenian. Marušič 2016 is a course on Standard Slovenian syntax (Univerza v Novi Gorici). The catalog record (webcat) codes Slovene as 'lexical' on Greenberg 2006; READALL_TARGETS lists the catalog rule field as empty (src qs-tier-2026-09-12).

new_statements.quote: Stress may either occur on the root syllable or on the theme-vowel: however, the phonological properties of the formed word have no clear correlation with stress assignment, which implies that these different positions of stress assignment do not seem to be triggered by any phonological factor. Rather, different stress patterns correlate either with specific roots, or with specific morphosyntactic constructions. This situates the regulation of stress assignment in NM Slovenian in the domain of morphosyntactic (i.e. lexical) specification. [pp. 49-50] [...] Similar to Standard Slovenian, NM Slovenian seems to place a tone on the stressed syllable of the word, but the final post-stressed syllable in the word bears a 'boundary tone', viz. it receives the opposite tone value of the one realized on the stressed syllable [p. 20]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (lexical, morphologically governed stress with pitch accent), stated for the Novo mesto dialect rather than the standard; adds the root-vs-theme stress classes, variable stress, the m.sg root-stress rule and the tone/boundary-tone description, and corroborates Greenberg 2003 and Šekli 2010 on morphological stress alternations in verbs.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Novo mesto (Dolenjska) Slovenian the position of stress is not set by any phonological factor: it is specified lexically by root and by morphological class/construction (root stress vs. theme-vowel stress in participles, with some roots variable between the two, e.g. ['jòkalá] ~ [jo'kàlá]); the masculine singular participle takes root stress by a morphological rule. A high or low tone is lexically specified on the stressed syllable and the word-final syllable carries the opposite, predictable boundary tone. Length is at best marginal and confined to stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only boundary tone on the word-final post-stressed syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Variable stress for some roots (jòk- 'cry' root or theme stress); m.sg participles take root stress even in theme-stressed paradigms except with some roots (kàd- 'smoke' allows theme stress in m.sg, dùb- 'get' does not).

tone_statements.quote: It is a general consensus in the field of Slovene studies that Slovene has two lexical tones, or pitch accents, historically termed acute and circumflex.1 The tones only appear in some (mainly central) Slovene dialects, and as an option also in the standard language. ... d. Contemporary Standard Slovene as spoken by educated speakers in Ljubljana is tonal ... Instead, High vs. Low is distributed on the head of the Prosodic Word (i.e. the stressed vowel) and the right edge of the Prosodic Word.
tone_statements.locator: p. 195 sec. 1 Introduction; p. 203 sec. 4 conclusion (3d); p. 204 sec. 4
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tone classes (acute/circumflex, 'or pitch accents') on stressed words, realised as High vs Low on stressed vowel and final syllable; stress independent; F0 study, 6 Ljubljana speakers.

Authors' open preprint:https://phonologist.org/papers/becker_jurgec_tone_atr_squib.pdf
tone_statements.quote: Žiri can be characterized as a pitch-accented variety of Slovenian. ... In the case of Žiri, tone is dependent on vowel length, vowel quality, and word size. Tone furthermore determines the position of stress. ... We propose that only High tone is phonologically active (3), as in BCMS. For the falling contours, the High tone is associated with the first mora, whereas for the rising contours, the High tone is linked to the second mora. Short vowels are monomoraic and have a single High tone. ... (3) Tonal contrasts in monosyllables Long Falling Long Rising Short
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, sec. 2 (opening paragraph) and p. 4, sec. 2.3 'Monosyllables', ex. (3)
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent: only H is phonological; H on 1st vs 2nd mora of a long vowel = Long Falling vs Long Rising, short vowels bear H; stress on leftmost H; floating H posited for retracting stems (sec. 3).

tone_statements.citation: Jurgec, Peter. 2007. Acoustic Analysis of Tones in Contemporary Standard Slovene: Preliminary Findings. Slovenski jezik / Slovene Linguistic Studies 6: 195-207. doi:10.3986/sls.6.1.10 (also KU ScholarWorks doi:10.17161/sls.1808.4418); open PDFhttps://ojs.zrc-sazu.si/sjsls/article/download/14265/12370
tone_statements.quote: This study was performed as a means of confirming or refuting Zorko’s claims about an unusually archaic prosodic system in Haloze. On the one hand, the phonetic analysis did show that quantity is distinctive in eastern Haloze. ... On the other hand, although the situation is not completely as one might expect for a Styrian dialect, there is no distinctive tone in Haloze. There is only one pattern of pitch contour on short syllables. It is rising. ... I discovered that the exact same pattern of pitch contour occurred on long as the one found on short.
tone_statements.locator: p. 177, 'Analysis of Meje in Haloze: Results', last sentence from p. 178 top
tone_statements.summary: Acoustic study: Haloze Slovene has no distinctive tone, one rising contour on all stressed syllables; free phonemic stress, distinctive length. Tonemic Slovene dialects given 2 tones, high vs low.

tone_statements.citation: Lundberg, Grant H. 2002. Circumflex Advancement in Haloze. Slovene Studies: Journal of the Society for Slovene Studies 19(1). doi:10.7152/ssj.v19i1.4052 (DOI registered by University of Washington Libraries; target journals.lib.washington.edu/index.php/ssj/article/view/4052 returned 404 on 2026-09-22; back issues reportedly mirrored on KU ScholarWorks, not verified).
tone_statements.quote: V slovenskem knjižnem jeziku se dopuščata dva tipa naglasa: dinamični in tonemski. Pri tonemskem naglaševanju ločimo na naglašenih vokalih dve intonaciji, ki ju tradicionalno imenujemo rastoča in padajoča. ... ju je bolje imenovati kar po znakih, s katerima ju označujemo: akutirana namesto rastoča in cirkumflektirana namesto padajoča. Cirkumflektirana intonacija je fonološko neoznačen tonem, akutirana pa označen (markiran) ... Ker je tonemsko naglaševanje v slovenskem knjižnem jeziku samo fakultativno, se mu navadno ne posveča dosti pozornosti.
tone_statements.translation: In the Slovene standard language two types of accent are admitted: dynamic and tonemic. In tonemic accentuation we distinguish on the stressed vowels two intonations, traditionally called rising and falling. ... it is better to name them simply after the signs with which we mark them: acute instead of rising and circumflex instead of falling. The circumflex intonation is the phonologically unmarked toneme, the acute the marked one ... Since tonemic accentuation is only optional in the Slovene standard language, it is usually not given much attention.
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemes (acute, circumflex) on the stressed vowel; tonemic accent optional beside dynamic; final/only short syllables circumflex only; at least ~600 tone-marked forms in the paradigms.

tone_statements.citation: Lundberg, Grant H. 2001. Typology of Tone Loss in Haloze, Slovenia: An Acoustic and Autosegmental Analysis. Slovenski jezik / Slovene Linguistic Studies 3: 169-189. doi:10.3986/sls.3.1.09; open PDFhttps://ojs.zrc-sazu.si/sjsls/article/download/14219/12340(also KU ScholarWorks).
tone_statements.quote: Standard Slovene distinguishes rising and falling tone in long syllables. Quantity outside of the stressed syllable has been lost, and all non-final stressed syllables have been lengthened. This means that short stress is only found on the final syllable of a word. In final position the original acute and the neo-acute on etymologically short vowels are short falling. ... The original circumflex in Slovene is realized as long and falling ... The northeastern Slovene dialects discussed here do not have distinctive pitch oppositions.
tone_statements.locator: p. 64, opening paragraph; last sentence from p. 69 footnote 2
tone_statements.summary: Historical accentology: Standard Slovene has rising vs falling tone on long (stressed) syllables; the Haloze/NE Slovene dialects documented have lost pitch (marks = length).

tone_statements.citation: Vermeer, Willem. 1986. Some sandhi phenomena involving prosodic features (vowel length, stress, tone) in Proto-Slavic, Serbo-Croatian, and Slovenian. In Henning Andersen (ed.), Sandhi Phenomena in the Languages of Europe, 577–604. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
tone_statements.quote: This paper focuses on the nominal system of Standard Slovenian, as it is spoken in Ljubljana (henceforth, Slovenian), also the dialect of the alphabetically second author. Slovenian contrasts two tones on the stressed syllable, High and Low, as in (1). (1) "pót ‘path’ "pòt ‘sweat’ ... In stressed syllables, the unmarked vowels {a, e, i, o, u} can appear with either a High or a Low tone anywhere a stressed vowel is allowed. ... In Slovenian, only one tone per Prosodic Word is allowed
tone_statements.locator: preprint p. 4 sec. 2 'The nominal system of Slovenian' and p. 5 (secs. 2-3) (published chapter pp. 11-26 paginates differently)
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones, High vs Low, contrasting only on the stressed syllable (one tone per prosodic word); floating suffixal H; Low forced on lax mid vowels; loanwords High only; 80+ marked forms.

tone_statements.citation: Neweklowsky, Gerhard. 1973. Slowenische Akzentstudien: Akustische und linguistische Untersuchungen am Material slowenischer Mundarten aus Kärnten. Wien: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.
tone_statements.quote: Dobro znano je, da ima slovenski jezik (njega del seveda) tonemsko nasprotje, npr. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) besede lipa (Nsg). Čeprav sta ta dva naglasna načina — prvega bomo imenovali akutiranega, drugega cirkumflektiranega — bila ugotovljena že pred več kot 150 leti ... je treba vendarle reči, da v svojem jedru vse do danes fonetično nista zadovoljivo pojasnjena. ... Desto wichtiger ist Mitja Sovre's Feststellung, dass der Gegensatz zwischen dem Akut und dem Zirkumflex als Tonhöhenunterschied aufzufassen ist.
tone_statements.translation: It is well known that Slovene (part of it, of course) has a tonemic opposition, e.g. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) of the word lipa (Nsg). Although these two accent types — we shall call the first acute, the second circumflex — were established more than 150 years ago ... it must be said that at their core they have to this day not been satisfactorily explained phonetically. ... All the more important is Sovre's finding that the opposition between acute and circumflex is to be understood as a pitch-height difference.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemic accents (acute, circumflex) on long stressed syllables; author: contrast is pitch height (acute low, basic shape concave; circumflex high, convex), shapes vary with sentence intonation; short stress only delimitative.

tone_statements.citation: Toporišič, Jože. 1968. Liki slovenskih tonemov [The shapes of the Slovene tonemes]. Slavistična revija 16 (1968) [pp. 315-393 per citing reference, not verified]. Ljubljana: Slavistično društvo Slovenije. Open scan: dLib.si URN:NBN:SI:DOC-VEQ4LZY1 (PDF 6.8 MB + TXT).
tone_statements.quote: ...the Standard Slovene language is characterized not only by the dynamic but also by the so-called tonemic word accentuation (or intonation rather), also referred to as 'pitch accent'. ... It should be pointed out that in statements the acute (marked below as A) is realized as a rising-falling tone ... when the circumflex (marked below as C), which is realized in statements as a falling tone, is used instead of the acute, this is seldom noticed by tonemic speakers ... This shows, of course, that the circumflex is the default ('unmarked') tone, while the acute is the 'marked' tone.
tone_statements.locator: Summary, p. 23 + section 3 'Acceptability of tonemic intonation..', p. 27
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two word accents: marked acute (rising-falling in statements) vs default circumflex (falling), codified beside 'dynamic' accentuation; only in some dialect areas; both tend to level to a fall.

tone_statements.quote: IZVLEČEK: V članku so obravnavani tonemski naglasni tipi glagola v (knjižni) slovenščini tako s sinhronega kot z diahronega gledišča. ... 1.1.1 Tip lẹ́sti lệzem z akutom na korenu v nedoločniku in s cirkumfleksom na korenu v sedanjiku podobno kot tip bíti bȋjem odraža psl. naglasni tip a
tone_statements.translation: ABSTRACT: The article treats the tonemic accent types of the verb in (standard) Slovene from both the synchronic and the diachronic viewpoint. ... 1.1.1 The type lesti lezem, with an acute on the root in the infinitive and a circumflex on the root in the present, like the type biti bijem, reflects Proto-Slavic accent type a
tone_statements.summary: Standard Slovene verb accent classes in tonemic notation (acute vs circumflex, also short-accented forms like lȅst); tonemic system presupposed, not counted; no phonetics; 74+ forms on p. 33 alone.

tone_statements.quote: The paper deals with the problem of relevant elements in the acoustic picture ( = image) of Slovene tonemes: of the acute accent ... and of the circumflex ... An opinion has prevailed recently which is for some positions an already established one, that there is a contrast in the Slovene tonemes between low and high, i.e. the contrast between the acute accent and the circumflex. ... A general result of the study: The main relevant element of the opposition between the acute accent and the circumflex is the difference in the realized height of the arsis

sources.quote: Stress may either occur on the root syllable or on the theme-vowel: however, the phonological properties of the formed word have no clear correlation with stress assignment, which implies that these different positions of stress assignment do not seem to be triggered by any phonological factor. sources.quote: In the illustrative wordlists and the transcribed passage below certain syllables have been marked as stressed. These stressed syllables are characterized by greater duration as well as by amplitude and pitch prominence. Non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable. Stress placement is not predictable but is also rarely distinctive in Slovene, although in a few instances different forms of the same noun or verb differ only in stress placement, e.g.: ['stua:ri], [stua'ri:], stvari ('things', dual vs plural), ['no:simo], [no'si:mo], nosimo ('carry' 1st p. pl. indicative and imperative). [p. 88] Standard Slovene distinguishes two pitch accents, traditionally referred to as the 'acute' and the 'circumflex' accents, and these accents are tied to the location of stress. [p. 89]

sources.quote: This study was performed as a means of confirming or refuting Zorko’s claims about an unusually archaic prosodic system in Haloze. On the other hand, although the situation is not completely as one might expect for a Styrian dialect, there is no distinctive tone in Haloze. sources.quote: V slovenskem knjižnem jeziku se dopuščata dva tipa naglasa: dinamični in tonemski. Pri tonemskem naglaševanju ločimo na naglašenih vokalih dve intonaciji, ki ju tradicionalno imenujemo rastoča in padajoča. ... ju je bolje imenovati kar po znakih, s katerima ju označujemo: akutirana namesto rastoča in cirkumflektirana namesto padajoča. tone.translation: In the Slovene standard language two types of accent are admitted: dynamic and tonemic. In tonemic accentuation we distinguish on the stressed vowels two intonations, traditionally called rising and falling. ... it is better to name them simply after the signs with which we mark them: acute instead of rising and circumflex instead of falling. The circumflex intonation is the phonologically unmarked toneme, the acute the marked one ... Since tonemic accentuation is only optional in the Slovene standard language, it is usually not given much attention.

sources.quote: Standard Slovene distinguishes rising and falling tone in long syllables. Quantity outside of the stressed syllable has been lost, and all non-final stressed syllables have been lengthened. This means that short stress is only found on the final syllable of a word. In final position the original acute and the neo-acute on etymologically short vowels are short falling. ... The original circumflex in Slovene is realized as long and falling ... The northeastern Slovene dialects discussed here do not have distinctive pitch oppositions.
sources.locator: p. 64, opening paragraph; last sentence from p. 69 footnote 2
sources.note: Historical accentology: Standard Slovene has rising vs falling tone on long (stressed) syllables; the Haloze/NE Slovene dialects documented have lost pitch (marks = length).

tone.translation: It is well known that Slovene (part of it, of course) has a tonemic opposition, e.g. lipo (Asg) — lîpo (Isg) of the word lipa (Nsg). Although these two accent types — we shall call the first acute, the second circumflex — were established more than 150 years ago ... it must be said that at their core they have to this day not been satisfactorily explained phonetically. ... All the more important is Sovre's finding that the opposition between acute and circumflex is to be understood as a pitch-height difference.

tone.quote: The paper deals with the problem of relevant elements in the acoustic picture ( = image) of Slovene tonemes: of the acute accent ... and of the circumflex ... An opinion has prevailed recently which is for some positions an already established one, that there is a contrast in the Slovene tonemes between low and high, i.e. the contrast between the acute accent and the circumflex. ... A general result of the study: The main relevant element of the opposition between the acute accent and the circumflex is the difference in the realized height of the arsis

tone.quote: This paper focuses on the nominal system of Standard Slovenian, as it is spoken in Ljubljana (henceforth, Slovenian), also the dialect of the alphabetically second author. Slovenian contrasts two tones on the stressed syllable, High and Low, as in (1). (1) "pót ‘path’ "pòt ‘sweat’ ... In stressed syllables, the unmarked vowels {a, e, i, o, u} can appear with either a High or a Low tone anywhere a stressed vowel is allowed. ... In Slovenian, only one tone per Prosodic Word is allowed
tone.locator: preprint p. 4 sec. 2 'The nominal system of Slovenian' and p. 5 (secs. 2-3) (published chapter pp. 11-26 paginates differently)
tone.summary: Two lexical tones, High vs Low, contrasting only on the stressed syllable (one tone per prosodic word); floating suffixal H; Low forced on lax mid vowels; loanwords High only; 80+ marked forms.
